newsitem.title: USA: Caribbean, Florida glad American strike averted.
newsitem.headline: Caribbean, Florida glad American strike averted.

text.p: Tourist officials in Miami and across the Caribbean breathed a sigh of relief on Saturday that a strike had been averted at American Airlines, which brings hoardes of high-spending visitors to the region during its peak winter holiday season.

"We're delighted and pleased that they will be staying at the bargaining table," Mayco Villafana, director of communications for Greater Miami Convention and Visitors Bureau, said. "Today we are very relieved."

President Bill Clinton intervened early on Saturday to stop a pilots' walkout at American, creating a 60-day cooling-off period as a presidential emergency board seeks a compromise in their contract dispute.

For tourism officials ready to welcome winter sun-seekers, the presidential order was a reprieve from what could have been an economic disaster. American is the main airline serving the Caribbean and accounts for 47 percent of the flights at Miami International Airport in Florida, which hit the height of its winter tourist season with the three-day weekend marking U.S. Presidents Day on Monday.

"If we looked at a period of a month, conservatively it would have cost close to $300 million in lost wages, in lost taxes, in lost expenditures by visitors who would not have been able to travel to the destination," Villafana said.
Tourist officials throughout the Caribbean had appealed to Clinton to intervene as they scrambled to minimize losses.
The Dominican Republic's tourism ministry had discussions with U.S. air companies to arrange charter service to replace American, the only air carrier to many Dominican resorts.

In the U.S. Virgin Islands, which also rely heavily on the Dallas-based carrier, the general manager of the Doubletree Sapphire Beach Resort had gone as far as lining up boats to carry any stranded visitors across the sea to Puerto Rico.
"The impact would have been tremendous," Beverly Nicholson, executive director of the St. Thomas-St. John Hotel Association in the U.S. Virgin Islands, said.

In a report issued on Friday, the U.S. territory's Tourism Department estimated that an American strike would keep 53 percent of weekly visitors, or about 8,000 people, away, with a revenue loss estimated at $1.1 million a day.

In Puerto Rico, American's Caribbean hub, the strike would have meant the loss of 52 flights daily at the height of the tourist season. Industry officials had estimated that American carried 70 percent of overnight visitors to the island.

"Nobody wants a strike so we are really relieved. But we had a contingency plan in case," said Luis Rosario, guest services manager at the Holiday Inn Crowne Plaza Hotel and Casino in the tourist district of Isla Verde near San Juan.
"Things are quiet and all back to normal today," he said.
